name: Estonia

facts.religion: No religion about 58%, Orthodox about 16%, Lutheran about 8%

snapshot: The digital republic on NATO's eastern edge elected a new president, constitutional watchdog Ülle Madise, in 2026, while its governing coalition struggles in the polls.
culture: Estonia's Song Festival, where some 30,000 singers perform together, helped drive the "Singing Revolution" that won independence from the Soviet Union in 1991. Saunas, especially the smoke sauna of the south, are UNESCO-listed. Estonian is related to Finnish, not to its Baltic neighbours' languages. Tallinn's medieval old town is one of Europe's best preserved.
society: Estonia runs almost all public services online, including voting, and produced Skype and many startups. About a quarter of the population is ethnic Russian, concentrated in Narva and Tallinn. Defence spending is among NATO's highest, reflecting fear of Russia. Tax rises to fund defence have hurt the government's popularity.
situation: Kristen Michal of the Reform Party became prime minister in 2024 after Kaja Kallas left to become the EU's foreign policy chief. In September 2026, parliament elected Ülle Madise, the chancellor of justice, as president, succeeding Alar Karis; she was sworn in on 12 October. Michal's Reform-Eesti 200 coalition lost its majority in August 2026 and now holds 50 of 101 seats. A parliamentary election is due in March 2027.
power: A parliamentary republic. The prime minister leads the majority in the 101-seat Riigikogu; the president is elected by parliament or an electoral college and is largely ceremonial.
